grammar.title: Future continuous & future perfect
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Future continuous: will be + -ing** → ação **em andamento** num momento do futuro:
- "This time tomorrow, I**'ll be flying** to Lisbon." (estarei voando)
- "Don't call at 8 — we**'ll be having** dinner."
- **Perguntas educadas** sobre planos (sem pressionar): "**Will you be using** the car tonight?" (soa menos invasivo que "Will you use...?")
- Coisas que vão acontecer **naturalmente / como rotina**: "I**'ll be seeing** Ana at work anyway, so I'll give her the book."

**Future perfect simple: will have + particípio** → ação **concluída até** um ponto do futuro:
- "**By** 2030, I**'ll have finished** my master's." (terei terminado)
- "By the time you arrive, we**'ll have eaten**."
- Negativa: "I **won't have finished** by Friday."
- Com **by**: by then, by the time, by next year, by the end of the month

**Future perfect continuous: will have been + -ing** → **duração** até um ponto do futuro:
- "In June, I**'ll have been working** here **for** five years." (farei cinco anos)
- "By the time she retires, she**'ll have been teaching for** 35 years."

**Lembre:** em time clauses (when, by the time, as soon as), use o **presente**: "By the time you **arrive** (❌ will arrive), we'll have left."

examples.en: This time next year, I'll be working remotely from a small town by the sea.

examples.pt: Mês que vem, faremos dez anos morando neste apartamento.

grammar.tip_pt: **Will you be + -ing?** é uma forma muito educada de perguntar sobre planos sem parecer um pedido: "**Will you be coming** to the meeting?" (só quer saber) x "**Will you come** to the meeting?" (soa como convite/pedido).

pronunciation.focus: Formas fracas: will have / will have been
pronunciation.tip_pt: Na fala, **will have** vira "**'ll've**" ("áiláv"): "I'll have finished" = "áilav FÍ-nisht". **Will have been** vira "**áilavbin**". A força fica no verbo principal e no tempo: "By **JUNE**, I'll've been **WORK**ing here for **FIVE** years."

dialogue.title: Career coaching session
dialogue.context_pt: Uma coach de carreira ajuda um cliente a planejar os próximos cinco anos.

lines.speaker: Coach
lines.en: So, Rodrigo, let's think long-term. Where do you see yourself five years from now?

lines.speaker: Rodrigo

lines.speaker: Coach

listening.title: The future of careers
listening.context_pt: Um futurista fala sobre como as carreiras devem mudar até 2035.

lines.speaker: Futurist
lines.en: Let me paint a picture of 2035. By then, many of the jobs we know today will have changed dramatically — and some will have disappeared altogether. Millions of people will be working in roles that don't exist yet. Most of us won't be doing the same job for forty years; instead, we'll be retraining several times throughout our careers. By the time today's teenagers retire, they'll probably have had five or six different careers, not just different jobs. AI tools will be handling many routine tasks, which means humans will be focusing more on creativity, empathy and complex problem-solving. The question isn't whether your job will change. It's whether you'll have learned how to keep learning.

questions.q: What will humans be focusing on?

reading.title: The 100-year life
reading.text: In their book The 100-Year Life, Lynda Gratton and Andrew Scott argue that as life expectancy increases, the traditional three-stage life — education, work, retirement — will no longer make sense for many people. If you're likely to live to 90 or 100, you probably won't be able to stop working at 60 and live on your savings for forty years. Instead, the authors predict a multi-stage life. People will be studying, working, taking breaks and retraining in different combinations throughout their lives. Someone might work in finance until 40, take a year off to travel, retrain as a teacher and then set up a small business at 60. By the time they finally retire, they will have had several careers, not one. This has big implications. Governments will need to rethink pensions and education. Companies will have to stop seeing older workers as a cost and start seeing them as an asset. And individuals will need to invest in what the authors call "intangible assets": skills, health, relationships and the ability to adapt. The good news? A longer life means more time to try new things. The challenge is that most of our institutions were designed for a much shorter one.

questions.answer: Education, work, retirement.

questions.q: Why won't it make sense for many people?

questions.q: What is a multi-stage life?

questions.q: What are "intangible assets"?
questions.answer: Skills, health, relationships and the ability to adapt.

writing.model:
My five-year plan

Five years from now, I hope I'll be working as a product manager at an international tech company, ideally in a hybrid role that allows me to spend part of the year in Brazil.

To get there, I've set myself several milestones. By the end of this year, I'll have completed this English course and taken the B2 First exam. Over the next twelve months, I'll be taking an online certificate in product management, which I'll be studying for every evening after work.

By the middle of 2027, I'll have been working in my current company for four years, and I'll have led at least two product launches. That experience should make my CV much stronger. I also plan to start applying for international positions at that point.

Of course, plans change. If I don't get an international job by 2028, I won't see it as a failure. I'll have gained valuable skills anyway, and I'll be in a better position than I am today.

Outside work, I want to look after my health. By the time I turn 35, I'd like to have run my first half marathon. In five years' time, I'll have been running regularly for almost a decade — which is a goal in itself!

grammar.title: Future in the past
grammar.explanation_pt:
Quando contamos uma história no passado, às vezes precisamos falar do que era **futuro naquele momento**. O inglês usa as formas de futuro "no passado":

**1. was/were going to + verbo** → plano ou intenção passada (geralmente **não** aconteceu):
- "I **was going to** call you, but I forgot." (eu ia te ligar)
- "We **were going to** move to Portugal, but then the pandemic happened."

**2. would + verbo** → previsão ou expectativa vista do passado (o "will" do passado):
- "I **knew** you **would** understand." (eu sabia que você entenderia)
- "She **promised** she **would** help." / "Nobody **thought** the company **would** survive."
- Também para narrar o destino: "He moved to London in 1990. He **would** never return to Brazil." (nunca mais voltaria)

**3. was/were about to + verbo** → algo **iminente** no passado (estava prestes a):
- "I **was about to** give up when I got the job offer."
- Mais formal: **was on the point of** + -ing: "She **was on the point of** resigning."

**4. was/were supposed to + verbo** → o que estava **combinado/esperado** (e geralmente não aconteceu):
- "The package **was supposed to** arrive yesterday."

**5. was/were + -ing** (present continuous no passado) → compromisso marcado no passado: "I couldn't meet him because I **was flying** to Recife the next day."

**6. was/were to + verbo** (formal/narrativo) → algo destinado a acontecer: "It was 2005. She **was to become** one of Brazil's greatest athletes."

listening.title: The interview that almost didn't happen
listening.context_pt: Uma profissional conta num podcast como quase perdeu a entrevista do emprego dos sonhos.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.en: The interview was supposed to start at 10 a.m. in São Paulo, and I was flying in from Curitiba that morning. Everything was going to be fine — I had planned it perfectly. Then the flight was delayed by three hours. I was about to call the company to cancel when I had an idea: I asked if we could do the interview by video from the airport. I honestly thought they would say no. But they agreed! So there I was, in a quiet corner of the departure lounge, with my laptop on my suitcase. I didn't know it then, but that interview would change my life. Two weeks later, I got the job — and my future boss told me that my calm reaction to the chaos was exactly what they were looking for.

reading.title: The plans that failed — and the success that followed
reading.text: Many famous success stories begin with a plan that went wrong. In the early 2000s, a small company called Odeo was going to become a major podcasting platform. Then Apple added podcasts to iTunes, and the founders realized their product would never compete. Instead of giving up, they held a brainstorming session, and one employee suggested a simple service for sharing short status updates. That idea became Twitter. Similarly, the founders of Slack were originally building an online game called Glitch. The game failed, but the internal chat tool the team had built to communicate turned out to be far more valuable than the game itself. Nobody at the time thought it would become one of the most widely used workplace tools in the world. Psychologists say that people who handle these moments well tend to share two qualities: they're flexible enough to change direction, and they see failure as information rather than as a final verdict. In other words, the plan you were going to follow might not be the plan you were supposed to follow. Sometimes, the most important skill is knowing when to let go.

writing.model:
The plan that changed my life

In 2020, I had everything planned. I was going to finish my engineering degree, get a job at a big construction company and buy an apartment by the time I was 30. My parents were proud, and I was sure it would all work out perfectly.

Then the pandemic came. The internship I was supposed to start in April was called off, and the company I had dreamed of working for stopped hiring. For months, I stayed at home, applying for jobs that never replied. At one point, I was on the point of giving up on engineering altogether.

To keep myself busy, I started making short videos explaining maths problems for my younger cousin. I posted a few online, never imagining that anyone would watch them. Within six months, my channel had 50,000 subscribers. Students from all over Brazil were writing to thank me.

I didn't know it then, but those videos would become my career. Today, I run an online education company with a team of twelve people. I still use my engineering skills every day — just not in the way I was going to.

Looking back, the cancelled internship turned out to be a blessing in disguise. If you're facing a plan that's fallen through, my advice is simple: stay curious. The plan you were going to follow might not be the best one for you.

grammar.title: Conditionals and language for negotiating
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Condições** (alternativas mais precisas ao if):
- **provided (that) / providing (that)** = desde que (formal) → "We can deliver by Friday, **provided that** you confirm the order today."
- **as long as / so long as** = contanto que → "You can work from home **as long as** you attend the Monday meeting."
- **on condition that** = sob a condição de que (muito formal)
- **unless** = a menos que → "We can't lower the price **unless** you order more units."
⚠️ Depois dessas expressões, use **presente simples** para o futuro (como com if).

**2. Propostas hipotéticas — second conditional** (soa mais flexível e menos ameaçador que o first):
- "**If we ordered** 500 units, **would** you **give** us a 10% discount?"
- "**What if we offered** a two-year contract?"
- "**Suppose** we paid upfront — **could** you deliver earlier?"

**3. Linguagem diplomática** (would, could, might, a bit, slightly, I'm afraid):
- "**We'd** like to propose..." / "**We'd be willing to**..."
- "That's **slightly higher than** our budget." (em vez de "too expensive")
- "**I'm afraid** we **wouldn't be able to** accept that."
- Perguntas negativas como sugestão: "**Wouldn't it make sense to**...?"

**4. Concessão em troca (if... then):**
"**If you could** extend the deadline, **we could** reduce the price by 5%." — nunca dê algo sem pedir algo em troca!

rows: We'd like to propose... / What if we...?
provided that / as long as / unless
If we ordered more, would you...?
I'm afraid that's slightly beyond our budget.
Could we meet halfway? / How about splitting the difference?
I think we've got a deal. / Let's put that in writing.

grammar.tip_pt: Na cultura de negócios anglo-saxã, um "**not**" seco soa agressivo. Prefira: "**I'm afraid that might be difficult**" ou "**That would be a challenge for us**" — o outro lado vai entender que é um não.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Em negociação, fale **devagar** e com **pausas** após números e condições: "We could offer... (pausa) ...eight thousand... (pausa) ...provided that...". A pausa transmite segurança. Evite subir a voz no final de propostas — soa inseguro.

listening.title: Salary negotiation tips
listening.context_pt: Uma recrutadora dá dicas de como negociar salário numa oferta de emprego.

lines.speaker: Recruiter
lines.en: Many people accept the first offer because they're afraid the company will withdraw it. In reality, most employers expect some negotiation, as long as you're polite and realistic. Here's my advice. First, research the market so you know your value. Second, never give the first number if you can avoid it — ask what the budget for the role is. Third, if the salary is lower than you hoped, try negotiating other things: extra vacation days, a training budget, remote work. You might say: "I'm very excited about the role. I was hoping for something closer to X. If the salary isn't flexible, would it be possible to discuss other parts of the package?" And finally, once you've reached an agreement, ask for everything in writing.

reading.title: Getting to Yes
reading.text: In 1981, Roger Fisher and William Ury of the Harvard Negotiation Project published Getting to Yes, a book that changed how many people think about negotiation. Instead of seeing negotiation as a battle where one side wins and the other loses, they proposed a method called "principled negotiation". It has four main ideas. First, separate the people from the problem: you can be tough on the issue while being respectful to the person. Second, focus on interests, not positions. A position is what someone says they want ("I want a 20% raise"); an interest is why they want it ("I need to pay for my children's school"). When you understand interests, creative solutions often appear — perhaps a smaller raise plus an education allowance. Third, invent options for mutual gain before deciding. Finally, insist on objective criteria, such as market prices or expert standards, rather than pure willpower. The authors also introduced the concept of BATNA — your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement. If you know what you'll do if the deal fails, you'll be much less likely to accept a bad one. Decades later, these ideas remain central to negotiation training around the world.

questions.q: How did Getting to Yes change the view of negotiation?
questions.answer: It replaced the idea of a battle with one winner with "principled negotiation".

questions.q: What's the difference between a position and an interest?
questions.answer: A position is what someone says they want; an interest is why they want it.

questions.q: What are "objective criteria"?
questions.answer: Standards like market prices or expert opinions, rather than willpower.

questions.q: What is a BATNA and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement; knowing it helps you avoid accepting a bad deal.

writing.model:
Subject: Re: Job offer – Senior Data Analyst

Dear Ms. Ferreira,

Thank you very much for offering me the position of Senior Data Analyst. I'm genuinely excited about the opportunity to join your team, especially the international expansion project we discussed.

Before accepting, I'd like to discuss two points. First, regarding the salary, the proposed figure is slightly lower than I had expected, based on my research for similar roles in the market and my eight years of experience. I was hoping for something closer to R$15,000. If that isn't possible, would you be willing to consider a review after six months, provided that I meet the agreed performance targets?

Second, I'm currently required to give 30 days' notice to my employer. Would it be possible to set my start date for March 3rd instead of February 15th? This would allow me to complete my current projects properly.

I'm confident that we can find an arrangement that works for both of us, and I look forward to your reply.

Kind regards,
Igor Santos

grammar.title: Meeting language by function
grammar.explanation_pt:
A linguagem de reuniões é altamente **funcional**: cada momento tem suas frases. Repare em como elas usam estruturas que você já domina (modais, perguntas indiretas, present perfect).

**ABRIR (chair):** "Shall we get started?" / "The **purpose** of today's meeting is to..." / "We have three **items** on the agenda." / "We've got 30 minutes, so let's keep it brief."

**DAR A PALAVRA:** "Ana, **would you like to** start?" / "**What are your thoughts on** this, Leo?" / "**We haven't heard from** Pedro yet."

**INTERROMPER com educação:**
- "**Sorry to interrupt, but**..." / "**Can I just come in here?**" / "**If I could just add something**..."
- Em reuniões online: "**Sorry, go ahead.**" (quando duas pessoas falam juntas)

**MANTER A PALAVRA:** "**If I could just finish** my point..." / "**Just one more thing**..." / "**Bear with me**..."

**DISCORDAR (com hedging do B2-M1!):** "**I see your point, but**..." / "**I'm not sure that would work because**..." / "**Have we considered**...?"

**CONTROLAR O RUMO E O TEMPO:**
- "**I think we're getting off track.** Let's get back to..."
- "**That's a good point, but maybe we could take it offline.**" / "**Let's park that for now.**"
- "**We're running out of time**, so let's move on."

**RESUMIR E DEFINIR AÇÕES (present perfect + will/going to):**
- "**So, to sum up**, we**'ve agreed** to... / we**'ve decided** that..."
- "**Action points:** Ana **will** send the report by Friday; Leo **is going to** contact the client."
- "**Who's going to** follow up on this?" / "**Let's touch base** next week."

grammar.tip_pt: Em reuniões online com estrangeiros, usar o botão **"raise hand"** e dizer "**Could I add something?**" é uma ótima estratégia para quem tem dificuldade de interromper. E sempre termine com **action points** claros: quem faz o quê até quando.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Para interromper, **aumente levemente o volume** na primeira palavra ("**SORRY** to interrupt...") e depois fale em ritmo normal. Uma interrupção hesitante e baixa é ignorada; uma alta demais soa agressiva. Pratique o equilíbrio!

listening.title: Why meetings fail
listening.context_pt: Um consultor de produtividade explica os erros mais comuns em reuniões.

lines.speaker: Consultant
lines.en: Surveys suggest that many professionals feel a large share of their meetings are unproductive. Why? In my experience, there are four main reasons. First, there's no clear purpose — people come without knowing what decision needs to be made. Second, the wrong people are invited: too many people, or not the ones who can actually decide. Third, nobody controls the discussion, so the conversation goes off track and the loudest voices dominate. And fourth — the most common — the meeting ends without clear action points. Everyone leaves thinking someone else will do the work. My rule is simple: no agenda, no meeting. And no meeting should end without three answers: what have we decided, who will do what, and by when.

questions.q: What is the first reason meetings fail?
questions.answer: There's no clear purpose.

questions.q: What problem is there with the people invited?
questions.answer: Too many people, or not the ones who can decide.

questions.q: What happens when nobody controls the discussion?
questions.answer: It goes off track and the loudest voices dominate.

questions.q: What three answers should every meeting end with?
questions.answer: What we've decided, who will do what, and by when.

reading.title: The silent participants
reading.text: In multinational companies, managers often notice a pattern: some team members — frequently non-native speakers — rarely speak up in meetings, even when they have excellent ideas. Research on international teams points to several reasons. One is language anxiety: the fear of making mistakes in front of colleagues, especially native speakers who talk quickly and use idioms. Another is cultural. In some cultures, interrupting is considered rude, and people wait for a pause that, in a fast-paced meeting, never comes. In others, junior employees are expected not to contradict senior ones publicly. The result is that companies lose valuable perspectives. Some organizations have started to change their meeting culture. Chairs are trained to invite quieter participants directly ("Marta, what's your view?"), agendas are shared in advance so people can prepare, and some meetings use a "round" format where everyone speaks in turn. Native speakers are encouraged to slow down and avoid slang. Non-native speakers, in turn, can benefit from learning a small set of phrases for entering a discussion. Ultimately, the goal is simple: the best idea should win — not the fastest speaker.

questions.q: Who often stays silent in multinational meetings?
questions.answer: Some team members, frequently non-native speakers.

questions.q: What are two reasons for this?
questions.answer: Language anxiety and cultural norms (e.g., interrupting is rude, juniors don't contradict seniors).

questions.q: What changes have some organizations made?
questions.answer: Chairs invite quieter participants, agendas are shared in advance, round formats are used.

questions.q: What is the ultimate goal, according to the text?
questions.answer: The best idea should win, not the fastest speaker.

speaking.instruction: Meeting simulation (20 min): groups of 4–5. One person chairs; the others receive role cards with different opinions on a real issue (e.g., the office moving to a new city, a four-day week, a new budget). Follow the agenda, interrupt politely, refocus, and end with clear action points.
speaking.instruction_pt: Simulação de reunião (20 min): grupos de 4–5. Uma pessoa conduz; as outras recebem cartões com opiniões diferentes sobre um tema real (ex.: mudança do escritório para outra cidade, semana de quatro dias, novo orçamento). Sigam a pauta, interrompam com educação, retomem o rumo e terminem com action points claros.

writing.task: Write the follow-up email (150–200 words) after a meeting: thank participants, summarize the main decisions, list the action points (who, what, when) and mention any issues parked for later.
writing.task_pt: Escreva o e-mail de seguimento (150–200 palavras) depois de uma reunião: agradeça aos participantes, resuma as principais decisões, liste os action points (quem, o quê, quando) e mencione assuntos deixados para depois.
writing.model:
Subject: Summary and action points – App launch meeting (May 6)

Hi everyone,

Thank you all for your input in today's meeting. Here's a quick summary of what we discussed and agreed.

Decisions
• We've agreed on a launch date of June 15th.
• The first version will include the payment and booking features only; the chat feature will be added in the second phase.
• Weekly progress meetings will take place every Thursday at 10 a.m.

Action points
• Kate will resend the final designs to the new shared folder by the end of today.
• Leo's team will start development on Monday, May 12th.
• Marta is going to prepare a testing plan by May 20th.
• I'll update the client and share the revised timeline by Wednesday.

Parked for later
• The marketing team's proposal to change the logo. I'll set up a separate meeting with them next week.

If I've missed anything or if anything is unclear, please let me know by tomorrow.

Best regards,
Paula

culture_note.title: "Let's circle back" e outros jargões
culture_note.text_pt: O inglês corporativo tem muitos jargões — alguns úteis, outros alvo de piadas: **circle back** (retomar depois), **touch base** (fazer contato rápido), **bandwidth** (disponibilidade: "I don't have the bandwidth"), **low-hanging fruit** (ganhos fáceis), **move the needle** (fazer diferença real). Entenda todos — mas use com moderação!

summary_pt: Abrir: Shall we get started? / The purpose of this meeting is to...
Interromper: Sorry to interrupt, but... / Can I just come in here?
Refocar: We're getting off track / Let's park that / take it offline.
Fechar: To sum up, we've agreed... + action points (who / what / when).

review.project_pt: **Business simulation:** em grupo, simulem o lançamento de um produto: (1) uma reunião de planejamento gravada (com pauta, interrupções e action points), (2) uma negociação com um "fornecedor" (outro grupo), (3) um e-mail de follow-up e (4) uma apresentação de 3 minutos com metas usando future perfect e future continuous.
